temptingClaims: Einstein's β is the ratio v/c.
whyTempting: Modern texts write β for \(v/c\), and the paper writes β in the formulas where speeds appear.
whereItIsTrue: The paper's β does depend only on the ratio of the speed \(v\) to the speed of light \(V\).

whatIsTrue.r0: In this paper β is the factor \(1/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), the one modern texts write γ. At 0.6 of the speed of light it is 1.25, not 0.6.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 3 ends with the transformation equations \(\tau = \beta\left(t - \frac{v}{V^2}x\right)\) and gives the moving system's coordinate along the motion as \(\beta(x - vt)\), and defines \(\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}}\) (p. 902). The speed of light is \(V\), not \(c\). So Einstein's β is the modern γ, and the modern β, \(v/c\), is his \(v/V\). SR-03's boost to 0.6 of the speed of light shows \(\beta = 1.25\).
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The paper's letters: \(v\) for the speed of the moving system, \(V\) for the speed of light. (2) Its definition: \(\beta = 1/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\) (p. 902). (3) At \(v = 0.6V\): \((v/V)^2 = 0.36\), \(1 - 0.36 = 0.64\), \(\sqrt{0.64} = 0.8\), so \(\beta = 1/0.8 = 1.25\). (4) A reader carrying the modern β = 0.6 into the paper's formulas gets every transformed coordinate wrong. (5) The notation concordance marks this collision in red on first use.
whatIsTrue.r3: Einstein's letters are kept on the source and translation faces. The explanation faces can switch to modern notation, where his β becomes γ; the switch renames a symbol and changes no argument.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 891–921 (1905), plate p. 902
